result.question: Native mobile interface design conventions a designer must decide for iOS and Android, current as of 2026 — platform design law only, not implementation code: (1) Apple's current design language and HIG direction 2025-2026 including Liquid Glass (iOS 26, WWDC 2025) — what it is, where it applies, what it demands, what Apple says not to do; (2) Google's Material 3 and Material 3 Expressive — status, what Expressive changed, stated research basis; (3) navigation models and when each is correct (iOS tab bar vs Android bottom nav, nav stack and back behavior incl. system back and predictive back, sheets and modals, NavigationSplitView vs navigation rail); (4) numeric specs (touch targets 44pt vs 48dp verified from primary sources, type scales and body sizes, spacing/margin baselines, corner radius); (5) safe areas and system regions (status bar, home indicator, Dynamic Island, display cutouts, edge-to-edge and Android 15+ mandatory edge-to-edge); (6) gesture systems and conflicts (iOS interactive pop gesture, Android back-swipe vs author-built horizontal swipe such as carousels and swipe-to-delete); (7) what genuinely differs such that one design cannot serve both, and where a cross-platform neutral design is legitimate. Primary sources only: developer.apple.com HIG, m3.material.io, developer.android.com.
result.summary: Split by source-of-truth first: one query aimed at Apple's HIG and one at Google's Material site, since pillars 1 and 2 are each single-vendor doctrine and the newest material (Liquid Glass, M3 Expressive) is heavily contaminated by blog restatement — dated, vendor-specific terminology filters for the primary page. The remaining three are cross-platform comparison queries, each forcing both platforms' primary docs into the same result set so the differences (pillar 7) fall out of the comparison rather than needing a separate speculative query: navigation and its gestures together (the back gesture is a navigation mechanism, and the carousel conflict is its failure mode), the numeric specs together (44pt vs 48dp must be verified side by side), and safe areas plus the Android 15 edge-to-edge mandate together.

results.title: Materials — Human Interface Guidelines (Apple)
results.snippet: The canonical designer-facing HIG page and the single best primary source for Pillar 1. Defines a material as "a visual effect that creates a sense of depth, layering, and hierarchy between foreground and background elements" and Liquid Glass as "a translucent surface that reflects and refracts light." Carries the explicit stacking prohibition: "When placing elements on top of Liquid Glass, avoid applying the material to both layers. Instead, use fills, transparency, and vibrancy for the top elements to make them feel like a thin overlay that is part of the material." Also documents the two variants (regular vs. clear) and the legibility burden clear glass imposes.

results.title: Adopting Liquid Glass — Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Apple's official adoption guide — the "what a designer must decide" companion to the Materials page. Covers where the material applies (controls, navigation, and system surfaces layered above content), what changes automatically when you build against the new SDK versus what you must redesign, and the restraint rule that Liquid Glass belongs to the navigation/control layer rather than the content layer. Primary source for the migration/decision framing rather than commentary.

results.title: Liquid Glass — Apple Developer Documentation (Technology Overview)
results.snippet: Apple's own definition of what Liquid Glass actually is: "a new digital meta-material that dynamically bends and shapes light," behaving "more like a lightweight liquid" and responding to touch. Establishes the unified cross-platform design language claim and the hardware/software blending rationale. This is the page to cite for the material's nature and behavior rather than any blog restatement.

results.title: Get to know the new design system — WWDC25 Session 356
results.snippet: Apple's primary session on the design system as a whole, and the source of the most quotable designer constraints: "Elements using Liquid Glass require clear separation from content to maintain legibility… controls sit on top of a system material, not directly on content. Without that separation, contrast can suffer." Also states the four design goals (blur hardware/software line, separate UI and navigation from content, make apps adaptable across window sizes, combine playfulness with sophistication) — directly answers what the new HIG direction demands.

results.title: Meet Liquid Glass — WWDC25 Session 219
results.snippet: The introduction talk from Apple's design team. Explains the two glass variants (regular, "designed to be legible by default," and clear, used in places like AVKit, which "requires more care to ensure legibility"), how tint and dynamic range shift automatically to keep controls legible, and the accessibility behavior a designer can rely on: Reduce Transparency makes the material frostier, Increase Contrast makes elements predominantly black or white with a contrasting border, Reduce Motion disables elastic properties — all automatic when using the system material.

results.title: Human Interface Guidelines (root) — Apple Developer
results.snippet: The living HIG index, updated for WWDC25 and the current 2025–2026 direction. Useful as the authoritative entry point to the platform-law pages this research needs beyond Liquid Glass — Materials, Color, Layout, Accessibility, and the platform-specific "Designing for iOS" and "Designing for iPadOS" pages that carry safe-area, Dynamic Island, and touch-target specifications. Apple describes the HIG as a living document of best practices, so it is the correct citation anchor for anything claimed as current.

results.title: Ensure compatibility with gesture navigation | Android Developers
results.snippet: The single most load-bearing primary source for the back-gesture-vs-author-swipe collision. States that Android's system back is an inward swipe from EITHER the left or right edge, that this 'might conflict with gestures that were previously used by app developers,' and names the two sanctioned mitigations: (1) go edge-to-edge and use system gesture insets (getSystemGestureInsets / mandatorySystemGestureInsets) to keep controls out of the reserved zones, and (2) View.setSystemGestureExclusionRects() (Android 10+, also in ViewCompat 1.1.0+) to selectively opt regions out of the back gesture — explicitly scoped to controls like drag handles and sliders, with a documented per-edge exclusion height cap so it cannot be abused to disable back wholesale. This is the page that tells a designer that a full-width carousel or swipe-to-delete row sitting under the edge zone is a real, documented defect and what the platform-approved fix is.

results.title: Predictive back design | Mobile | Android Developers
results.snippet: Apple has no equivalent of this, which is exactly why it matters for the 'what genuinely differs' pillar. Google's designer-facing (not code) spec for predictive back: the semantics of the peek/commit threshold, that the inner surface scales down as the gesture progresses and content swaps via fade-through once committed, and motion tokens (STANDARD_DECELERATE / PathInterpolator) so movement reads at the start of the drag. Critically it repeats the conflict rule from the design side: predictive back respects the gesture insets defined by edge-to-edge, and designers should 'avoid adding touch gestures or drag targets under these gesture areas.' Establishes that on Android, back is a previewable, cancellable, animated navigation state — a designed transition the designer owns, not a free system behavior.

results.title: Tab bars | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Primary source for the iOS side of the top-level navigation decision, and current for iOS 26 — the tab bar is now a floating Liquid Glass element that can shrink/hide on scroll and, on iPad, adapt into or coexist with a sidebar. Key designer law here: tab bars are for peer top-level sections only, tab selection must persist per-tab navigation state, tabs must never be used to perform actions, and you should avoid hiding or disabling tabs. This is the article that contrasts with Material's navigation bar and is the anchor for the 'iOS tab bar ≠ Android bottom nav' distinction (Apple caps practical tabs low and pushes overflow to a More tab; Material caps at 5 and forbids overflow).

results.title: Navigation rail – Material Design 3
results.snippet: Gives the numeric window-size law that decides bottom navigation bar vs navigation rail — the Android counterpart to iOS NavigationSplitView/sidebar adaptation. Compact windows (<600dp, phone portrait) must use the navigation bar; the collapsed rail is valid from 600dp–839dp (tablet/foldable portrait); the rail is called out as more ergonomic and visually balanced at larger sizes given hand placement. Hard constraint stated outright: never use the navigation rail and navigation bar simultaneously. This is a breakpoint-driven rule with no iOS equivalent — Apple switches on size class and idiom, Material switches on dp window-size class — and is a genuine 'one design cannot serve both' case.

results.title: Sheets | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: The iOS modal-presentation law. Covers when a sheet is correct (a scoped task closely related to the current context, retaining context of the parent) versus a full-screen modal or a pushed screen, plus detents/resizable heights, the drag-to-dismiss gesture and why a sheet that holds unsaved work must confirm before dismissing, and the iOS 26 Liquid Glass treatment where sheets pick up a glass edge and inherit the background's tint. Directly relevant to gesture conflict: a sheet's vertical drag-to-dismiss competes with scrollable content inside it, the same class of collision as horizontal edge-swipe vs carousel. Pair with the HIG's Modality article for the 'when is modality justified at all' rule.

results.title: Gestures | Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Apple's primary statement of iOS gesture law and the iOS half of the conflict analysis: standard system gestures (edge swipe back / interactive pop, swipe-up home indicator, Control/Notification Center pulls, Dynamic Island interactions) are reserved, and custom gestures must not redefine or interfere with them. Establishes that the interactive pop gesture is a user expectation the designer inherits — disabling it to make room for an author-built horizontal swipe is a regression, and the sanctioned pattern is to keep full-width horizontal swipe affordances (carousels, swipe-to-delete rows) out of the leading screen edge or make them inset. Note the page is JS-rendered, so it must be read in a browser rather than fetched as static text.

results.title: Expressive Material Design: Google Research (Google Design)
results.snippet: The primary, first-party statement of Expressive's research basis — verified by fetch: 46 separate research studies, 18,000+ participants, three years, hundreds of design iterations. Methods: eye tracking, surveys, focus groups, sentiment experiments, usability testing. Findings a designer can cite: key UI elements spotted up to 4x faster in Expressive designs (with faster tap times); older users spotted key interactive elements as fast as younger users across 10 apps tested (closing the usual age-usability gap); preference up to 87% among 18-24s and positive across all demographics; +32% perceived cultural relevance, +34% modernity, +30% innovation. This is the source the participant/study fingerprint traces back to — every blog restatement quotes these numbers from here.

results.title: Start building with Material 3 Expressive — Material Design 3
results.snippet: m3.material.io's own scoping statement of what Expressive is and what it changed: an expansion of Material Design 3 with research-backed updates to theming, components, motion, typography, shape and color. Names the concrete deltas a designer must decide on — 35 new shapes plus shape morphing in the Material Shapes Library (Figma Design Kit and Jetpack Compose), emphasized typography styles, new/expanded component variants. Note: m3.material.io is a JS-rendered SPA, so this page must be read in a browser rather than fetched as static HTML.

results.title: M3 Expressive: New Motion System (motion physics + motion theming) — Material Design 3
results.snippet: Primary source for the single biggest designer-facing change in Expressive: motion moves from duration-and-easing-curve to a physics/spring-based motion system. Defines the customizable motion scheme built from motion properties (overridable per product) and the two presets a designer must choose between — Expressive (Material's recommended default for most situations, hero moments and key interactions; overshoots final values to add bounce) and Standard. Introduced in the material3 1.4.0-alpha14 timeframe. This is the page that decides whether your spec says '300ms ease-out' or names a spring scheme.

results.title: Compose Material 3 release notes — Jetpack (developer.android.com)
results.snippet: The authoritative answer to 'what is Expressive's status in 2026', which no blog restatement gets right. Expressive APIs are still shipping in alpha: material3 1.5.0-alpha23 (1 July 2026) and 1.5.0-alpha24 (15 July 2026); when 1.4.0 went stable the Expressive APIs moved forward into the 1.5.0-alphaX line and are expected to go stable in 1.5.0. Recent alphas are still adding Expressive components (expressive TimePicker plus a scroll variant, new material3-ripple library, non-interactive list-item variants that follow Expressive specs while deprecating the non-expressive versions). Designers should treat Expressive as a published design spec whose Android implementation is still pre-stable.

results.title: Google launches Material 3 Expressive redesign for Android and Wear OS (blog.google)
results.snippet: First-party launch announcement establishing when and where Expressive actually shipped as product UI (Android and Wear OS), rather than as a spec. Useful for dating the rollout and for the platform-scope claim; thinner on the numeric spec detail than m3.material.io, so use it for status/provenance and defer to m3.material.io for the design law itself. Companion piece: android-developers.googleblog.com/2025/08/introducing-material-3-expressive-for-wear-os.html for the Wear-specific guidance.

results.title: Typography — type scale tokens (Material Design 3)
results.snippet: Primary source for the numeric type specifications the original question demands (pillar 4) and for the Expressive typography delta specifically. Carries the baseline M3 type scale tokens — display/headline/title/body/label at large/medium/small with their sizes, line heights, weights and tracking — plus the 15 emphasized type styles added in the Expressive update. Material's guidance is to use baseline and emphasized styles together to build hierarchy; shape is explicitly designed to echo type attributes, so the shape and type decisions are coupled. Also SPA-rendered — read in a browser to extract exact dp/sp values rather than fetching.

results.title: Behavior changes: Apps targeting Android 15 or higher — Android Developers
results.snippet: The primary, dated source for the mandatory edge-to-edge change: "Apps are edge-to-edge by default on devices running Android 15 if the app is targeting Android 15 (API level 35)." Also specifies the system-region consequences a designer must plan for: status bar transparent by default with setStatusBarColor()/R.attr#statusBarColor deprecated and non-functional; gesture nav bar transparent with setNavigationBarColor() no longer affecting it; 3-button nav bar at 80% opacity with contrast enforced by default; and display cutout forced open — layoutInDisplayCutoutMode of non-floating windows must be LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS, with SHORT_EDGES, NEVER and DEFAULT all reinterpreted as ALWAYS so no black cutout bar appears. This is the hard platform law behind pillar 5.

results.title: Behavior changes: Apps targeting Android 16 or higher — Android Developers
results.snippet: Closes the loophole and makes edge-to-edge unconditional: for apps targeting Android 16 (API 36), R.attr#windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement is deprecated and disabled and the app cannot opt out. Notes the split behavior (the opt-out still works for an API-36 app running on an Android 15 device, disabled on Android 16 devices) and advises removing it entirely. Essential for stating the 2026 status accurately: Android 15 enforced it with an escape hatch, Android 16 removed the escape hatch.

results.title: Edge-to-edge — Android design guidance (Layout and content)
results.snippet: Google's design-side (not code) rules for what may occupy which screen region — the closest match to "platform design law" for this pillar. States the core split: "backgrounds and divider lines should also draw edge-to-edge while content like text and buttons should be inset to avoid the system UI and hardware elements." Do/don't rules: draw background and scrolling content under system bars; solid app bar backgrounds and horizontal carousels should draw into the display cutout; inset critical UI using display cutout insets; never place critical UI at the very screen edge; "Avoid adding tap gestures or drag targets under system insets; these conflict with edge-to-edge and gesture navigation" (direct tie-in to pillar 6). Also scrim law: add a system bar scrim for three-button navigation when the bottom app bar animates away, keep gesture navigation transparent with no extra scrim, don't stack protections (e.g. M3 TopAppBar built-in plus a custom one), and use separate protections per pane in adaptive layouts.

results.title: Layout — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple's counterpart rule set for safe areas and system regions. Defines the safe area as the portion of a view unobscured by bars and other content, and frames it as the mechanism that keeps UI clear of rounded display corners, the Home indicator, and the Dynamic Island — all of which can otherwise overlap a control's tap target. Guidance for the Home indicator: avoid placing interface elements in close proximity, leave negative space around it, and keep all non-scrollable content inside the safe area (scrollable content may pass beneath). Notes the indicator adapts light/dark for contrast against whatever is behind it, so the designer owns the backdrop, not the indicator. Pair with the Android pages for the two-sided "what may never occupy which region" answer. (Page is JS-rendered — must be read in a browser, not fetched as text.)

results.title: About window insets — Jetpack Compose, Android Developers
results.snippet: The authoritative taxonomy of Android system regions a designer must name when specifying a screen — and it distinguishes visual from gestural safety, which is the bridge between pillars 5 and 6. safeDrawing "protect[s] content that shouldn't be drawn underneath any system UI"; safeGestures "protect[s] content with gestures... avoids system gestures clashing with app gestures (such as those for bottom sheets, carousels, or in games)"; safeContent is the union, ensuring "no visual overlap and no gesture overlap." Also enumerates the granular regions: statusBars, navigationBars, captionBar, systemBars, ime (keyboard), displayCutout (notches and pinholes), waterfall (curved edges), systemGestures (opt-out-able via systemGestureExclusion) and mandatorySystemGestures (not opt-out-able).

results.title: Support display cutouts — Android Developers
results.snippet: Primary reference for the cutout region itself: how Android defines a display cutout, the layoutInDisplayCutoutMode values (ALWAYS / SHORT_EDGES / NEVER / DEFAULT) and how cutout bounds are exposed, plus guidance that content must not be permanently obscured by the cutout and that cutout position varies by device and orientation. Useful as the Android analogue to Apple's Dynamic Island region, and it grounds why Android 15's forced reinterpretation of the cutout modes matters — the designer can no longer assume a letterboxed, cutout-free canvas.

results.title: Accessibility — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for the Apple half of the 44pt/48dp discrepancy. This is the HIG page that states the minimum hit-target rule ("at least 44x44 pt") alongside Apple's other numeric accessibility floors (Dynamic Type support, contrast). Caveat for whoever writes the report: developer.apple.com HIG pages are client-rendered — WebFetch returns only the <title>, so the body must be read in a real browser (the /browse skill) or cited from Apple's own Buttons/Layout pages, which restate the same 44x44 pt figure. Note the unit: Apple specifies *points*, not pixels or dp, and applies it to the touch region, not the drawn glyph.

results.title: Accessibility — Android Mobile UI design guides (developer.android.com)
results.snippet: Verified by direct fetch (this page does render, unlike m3.material.io). States plainly: minimum touch target 48 dp — "All touch targets must be at least 48 dp, even if this extends past the UI element's visual boundary" — plus minimum body text 12 sp, text contrast 4.5:1 and non-text/icon contrast 3:1. This is the cleanest citable Google-side source for the 48dp number and resolves the 44pt-vs-48dp question: the two platforms genuinely differ (44 pt ≈ 44 px @1x vs 48 dp ≈ 48 px @1x, roughly 9% larger), and the target may exceed the visual bounds on both. Related Android primary: developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/apps and the Compose api-defaults page (Material components already enforce 48dp; custom composables do not).

results.title: Typography — type scale tokens, Material Design 3
results.snippet: Canonical Material 3 type scale: 30 styles across the Display/Headline/Title/Body/Label roles, each with a single token carrying size, line height, weight and tracking, shared identically between design tools and code. Body Large = 16sp / 24sp line height / weight 400 — the Android body-text default to set against iOS Body at 17 pt. This is the source for pillar 4's "default type scales and body text sizes" on the Google side. Page is JS-rendered; use /browse to pull the full token table rather than WebFetch.

results.title: Typography — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple-side counterpart to the Material type scale: the iOS built-in text styles (Large Title, Title 1-3, Headline, Body, Callout, Subhead, Footnote, Caption 1-2) with their default point sizes, weights and leading — Body at 17 pt is the default reading size, and the HIG notes 17-point text as the reference size for iOS UI. Also the primary statement of Dynamic Type behavior: using system text styles opts you in automatically, and sizes scale past 200% at AX3 and past 300% for body text at AX5 — the number that actually constrains a designer's layout, not the static 17 pt. Companion primary source: developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/ for what Apple now audits.

results.title: Spacing — tokens, Material Design 3
results.snippet: Material 3's spacing baseline: all spacing tokens sit on a 4dp grid (the older 8dp grid is the M2-era phrasing; M3 tokenizes at 4dp increments), which is the number pillar 4 asks for on "spacing and margin baselines." Pair with the sibling primary pages the same searcher should pull: m3.material.io/styles/shape/corner-radius-scale for the corner-radius scale (the named shape levels Material uses for components, and the Expressive shape-morph additions) and m3.material.io/foundations/designing/structure for layout grid margins, gutters and pane structure — that structure page also restates the 48dp touch target. All three are JS-rendered and return only a title via WebFetch.

results.title: Layout — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple's answer to "margin and spacing baseline": Apple deliberately publishes no numeric grid equivalent to Material's 4dp tokens — it specifies safe areas, layout margins and readable content guides, plus device screen dimensions, and restates the 44x44 pt minimum for interactive elements. Useful precisely because it documents an asymmetry worth calling out in the final answer: Material gives a designer tokens to hit, Apple gives constraints to respect. Also the crossover source into pillar 5 (safe areas, margins that adapt across size classes). JS-rendered; read via browser. See also developer.apple.com/design/tips/ for Apple's own condensed dos-and-don'ts sheet, which repeats the 44x44 pt figure in a fetchable form.

claims.claim: Apple defines Liquid Glass as a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation (tab bars, sidebars) that floats above the content layer, establishing hierarchy while letting content scroll and peek through beneath it.
claims.quote: Liquid Glass forms a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation elements — like tab bars and sidebars — that floats above the content layer, establishing a clear visual hierarchy between functional elements and content. Liquid Glass allows content to scroll and peek through from beneath these elements to give the interface a sense of dynamism and depth, all while maintaining legibility for controls and navigation.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly prohibits using Liquid Glass in the content layer, directing designers to standard materials there; the only exception is transient interactive controls (sliders, toggles) which adopt a Liquid Glass appearance while active.
claims.quote: Don’t use Liquid Glass in the content layer. Liquid Glass works best when it provides a clear distinction between interactive elements and content, and including it in the content layer can result in unnecessary complexity and a confusing visual hierarchy. Instead, use standard materials for elements in the content layer, such as app backgrounds. An exception to this is for controls in the content layer with a transient interactive element like sliders and toggles; in these cases, the element takes on a Liquid Glass appearance to emphasize its interactivity when a person activates it.

claims.claim: Apple instructs designers to use Liquid Glass sparingly on custom controls — system components adopt it automatically, and overusing it on multiple custom controls degrades the experience; it should be limited to the most important functional elements.
claims.quote: Use Liquid Glass effects sparingly. Standard components from system frameworks pick up the appearance and behavior of this material automatically. If you apply Liquid Glass effects to a custom control, do so sparingly. Liquid Glass seeks to bring attention to the underlying content, and overusing this material in multiple custom controls can provide a subpar user experience by distracting from that content. Limit these effects to the most important functional elements in your app.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass ships in two variants — regular and clear. Regular blurs and adjusts background luminosity for legibility and is used by most system components (alerts, sidebars, popovers); clear is highly translucent and is only for components floating over visually rich media backgrounds, where a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity should be added if the underlying content is bright.
claims.quote: Only use clear Liquid Glass for components that appear over visually rich backgrounds. ... The regular variant blurs and adjusts the luminosity of background content to maintain legibility of text and other foreground elements. ... Use the regular variant when background content might create legibility issues, or when components have a significant amount of text, such as alerts, sidebars, or popovers. ... If the underlying content is bright, consider adding a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass appearance is not fully author-controlled: it changes in response to system settings including a user-selected preferred look and accessibility settings that reduce transparency or increase contrast — so designers must not choose a material for the color it appears to impart.
claims.quote: The appearance of these variants can differ in response to certain system settings, like if people choose a preferred look for Liquid Glass in their device’s settings, or turn on accessibility settings that reduce transparency or increase contrast in the interface. ... Avoid selecting a material or effect based on the apparent color it imparts to your interface, because system settings can change its appearance and behavior.

result.publishDate: Last updated September 9, 2025 (change log: \"September 9, 2025 — Updated guidance for Liquid Glass\"; \"June 9, 2025 — Added guidance for Liquid Glass\")

claims.claim: Liquid Glass is defined by Apple as a distinct functional layer that floats above app content to provide structure and clarity, not as a decorative surface treatment applied to content itself.
claims.quote: Liquid Glass defines a new functional layer in the UI, floating above your content to bring structure and clarity, without ever stealing focus.

claims.claim: Corner radius in the new system is governed by three defined shape types: fixed shapes (constant radius), capsules (radius = half the container height), and concentric shapes (radius = parent radius minus padding), with nested containers required to be concentric so the system can compute inner radii automatically.
claims.quote: Fixed shapes "have a constant corner radius"; capsules "use a radius that's half the height of the container"; concentric shapes "calculate their radius by subtracting padding from the parent's." ... "One place this often shows up in is nested containers—like artwork in a card. If something feels off, the answer is simple. Its shape probably needs to be concentric to allow the system to calculate the inner radii automatically."

claims.claim: Apple instructs designers to strip pre-existing custom bar decoration (extra backgrounds, borders on buttons) because the new system appearance supplies emphasis, and to apply Liquid Glass material to a custom control itself rather than to its inner views.
claims.quote: We've all added extra backgrounds or borders to give buttons the right weight. This was common, and totally valid, for a long time. But with the new system appearance, we're all relearning where emphasis comes from, making customizations like these unnecessary. ... When making custom controls, use the same approach, and make sure to apply the material directly to the control, not its inner views.

claims.claim: The iOS tab bar is reserved for persistent app-level destinations — screen-specific actions such as a checkout button must not be placed there — and iOS now includes a dedicated Search tab at the bottom of the tab bar.
claims.quote: Avoid placing screen-specific actions here—a checkout button, for example, belongs with the content it supports. Mixing elements from different parts of the UI can blur hierarchy and make it harder to distinguish what's persistent from what's contextual. ... That's why iOS now includes a dedicated Search tab at the bottom, making it quicker to access and easier to reach.

claims.claim: Scroll edge effects come in exactly two styles (soft, default and used mostly on iOS/iPadOS; hard, used mostly on macOS), are limited to one per view, must not be mixed or stacked, and must not be used where no floating UI elements exist — they are functional, not decorative overlays.
claims.quote: You'll see two styles across the system, soft and hard. You should avoid mixing or stacking them on top of each other. ... Apply one scroll edge effect per view. ... And remember, scroll edge effects are not decorative. They don't block or darken like overlays. They simply clarify where UI and content meet, and shouldn't be used where there aren't any floating UI elements.

claims.claim: Apple defines Liquid Glass as a single new dynamic material shared across all Apple platforms (not an iOS-only style), characterized by glass optics combined with fluidity.
claims.quote: Interfaces across Apple platforms feature a new dynamic material called Liquid Glass, which combines the optical properties of glass with a sense of fluidity.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass is applied by the system to standard controls and navigation elements automatically; it is an opt-in effect for custom elements, which means the designer's decision is where to add it beyond the control/navigation layer, not whether the standard chrome gets it.
claims.quote: Standard components from SwiftUI, UIKit, and AppKit like controls and navigation elements pick up the appearance and behavior of this material automatically. You can also implement these effects in custom interface elements.

claims.claim: Apple's stated design constraint for the Liquid Glass layer is color restraint: color in controls and navigation must be limited so those elements stay legible and the underlying content remains the visual focus.
claims.quote: Be judicious with your use of color in controls and navigation so they stay legible and allow your content to infuse them and shine through.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly states that adopting Liquid Glass is not a ground-up redesign — the prescribed path is recompiling against the latest SDK to inherit the material, then correcting the interface against best practices.
claims.quote: If you have an existing app, adopting Liquid Glass doesn’t mean reinventing your app from the ground up. Start by building your app in the latest version of Xcode to see the changes.

claims.claim: Apple pairs Liquid Glass with an edge-to-edge content model, providing a named 'background extension effect' and prescribing that horizontal scroll views extend under sidebars and inspectors.
claims.quote: Create an edge-to-edge content experience with the background extension effect.Enhance the edge-to-edge content experience by extending horizontal scroll views under a sidebar or inspector.

claims.claim: Apple defines Liquid Glass as a single new dynamic material shared across all Apple platforms, characterized by the optical properties of glass combined with fluidity — i.e. it is a material, not a style or theme.
claims.quote: Interfaces across Apple platforms feature a new dynamic material called Liquid Glass, which combines the optical properties of glass with a sense of fluidity. Learn how to adopt this material and embrace the design principles of Apple platforms to create beautiful interfaces that establish hierarchy, create harmony, and maintain consistency across devices and platforms.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass applies to the controls and navigation layer, not the content layer: standard SwiftUI/UIKit/AppKit controls and navigation elements adopt the material automatically, and only custom interface elements require explicit application.
claims.quote: Standard components from SwiftUI, UIKit, and AppKit like controls and navigation elements pick up the appearance and behavior of this material automatically. You can also implement these effects in custom interface elements.

claims.claim: Apple instructs designers to restrain color in controls and navigation under Liquid Glass, because the material is meant to let underlying content show through and tint it — saturating the glass layer is the named failure mode.
claims.quote: Be judicious with your use of color in controls and navigation so they stay legible and allow your content to infuse them and shine through.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass presumes an edge-to-edge content layout: Apple directs designers to extend content to the display edges using the background extension effect, and to run horizontal scroll views underneath sidebars and inspectors rather than inset from them.
claims.quote:
Create an edge-to-edge content experience with the background extension effect.

Enhance the edge-to-edge content experience by extending horizontal scroll views under a sidebar or inspector.

claims.claim: The Liquid Glass transition requires designers to rebuild the app icon as a set of simple, bold layers that render with dimensionality across devices and light/dark appearances, rather than reusing a flat single-image icon.
claims.quote: Reimagine your app icon with simple, bold layers that offer dimensionality and consistency across devices and appearances.

claims.claim: Apple restricts Liquid Glass to the navigation layer that floats above app content; applying it to content-layer elements (e.g. a table view) is explicitly discouraged because it muddies hierarchy.
claims.quote: You may be tempted to use Liquid Glass everywhere but it is best reserved for the navigation layer that floats above the content of your app. Consider this tableview: making it Liquid Glass would make it compete with other elements and muddy the hierarchy. So keep it in the content layer instead to ensure clarity.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits stacking Liquid Glass on Liquid Glass; elements placed on top of a glass surface must instead use fills, transparency, and vibrancy.
claims.quote: Always avoid glass on glass. Stacking Liquid Glass elements on top of each other can quickly make the interface feel cluttered and confusing. When placing elements on top of Liquid Glass, avoid applying the material to both layers. Instead, use fills, transparency, and vibrancy for the top elements to make them feel like a thin overlay that is part of the material.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass ships in exactly two variants — Regular (adaptive, the default for nearly all uses) and Clear (non-adaptive, permanently more transparent, valid only over media-rich content with a dimming layer and bold/bright content above) — and the two must never be mixed in the same interface.
claims.quote: Regular is the most versatile and the one you will be using the most. This variant gives you all the visual and adaptive effects we've talked about, and provides legibility regardless of context. It works in any size, over any content and anything can be placed on top of it. Clear, on the other hand, does not have adaptive behaviors. It is permanently more transparent... They should never be mixed, as they each have their own characteristics and specific use cases.

claims.claim: Tinting Liquid Glass is reserved for primary elements/actions only; Apple states that tinting every element destroys emphasis and that app color should live in the content layer instead.
claims.quote: Tinting should only be used to bring emphasis to primary elements and actions in the UI... Avoid tinting all your elements. When every element is tinted, nothing stands out, and it can be confusing. If you want to imbue color into your app, do it in the content layer instead.

claims.claim: Liquid Glass automatically honors three system accessibility settings — Reduced Transparency (frostier, obscures more background), Increased Contrast (predominantly black/white with contrasting border), and Reduced Motion (disables elastic properties) — with no per-app work required when the standard material is used.
claims.quote: Reduced Transparency: Makes Liquid Glass frostier and obscures more of the content behind it... These are available automatically whenever you use the new material. So whenever these settings are turned on at a system-level, Liquid Glass elements will get them across the board.

claims.claim: Android's system back gesture is an inward swipe from EITHER the left or the right screen edge (not left-only), so any author-built horizontal swipe affordance anchored to either vertical edge is in direct conflict with system back.
claims.quote: The new system gesture for back is an inward swipe from either the left or the right edge of the screen. This might interfere with app navigation elements in those areas.

claims.claim: The back-gesture conflict is resolved by selective, region-scoped opt-out rather than a global disable: the app declares a List<Rect> of regions that must receive touch input, via View.setSystemGestureExclusionRects() (Android 10 / API 29; also in ViewCompat since androidx.core:core:1.1.0-dev01). DrawerLayout and SeekBar do this automatically.
claims.quote: To maintain functionality of elements on the left and right edges of the screen, opt out of the back gesture selectively by indicating to the system which regions need to receive touch input. You can do this by passing a List<Rect> to the View.setSystemGestureExclusionRects() API introduced in Android 10. ... Note: The DrawerLayout and SeekBar components support automatic opt-out behavior out of the box.

claims.claim: The home and quick-switch gestures at the bottom of the screen CANNOT be opted out of by an app, unlike the back gesture — so a designer must keep interactive elements out of the bottom gesture zone rather than reclaim it; the only inset information available is WindowInsets.getMandatorySystemGestureInsets(), which reports touch-recognition thresholds.
claims.quote: The new system gestures for home and quick switch both involve swipes at the bottom of the screen in the space previously occupied by the nav bar. Apps can't opt out of these gestures as they can with the back gesture. To mitigate this problem, Android 10 introduces the WindowInsets.getMandatorySystemGestureInsets() API, which informs apps of the touch recognition thresholds.

claims.claim: Gesture-navigation compatibility on Android imposes exactly two obligations on an app, one of which is edge-to-edge content — establishing edge-to-edge as a requirement tied to gesture nav from Android 10 (API 29) onward, before the Android 15 mandatory enforcement.
claims.quote: Beginning with Android 10 (API level 29), the Android system supports fully gesture-based navigation. There are two things app developers must do to ensure their apps are compatible with this feature: Extend app content from edge to edge. Handle conflicting app gestures.

claims.claim: Predictive back was introduced in Android 13 (API level 33) as a multiyear rollout across phones, large screens and foldables, and its defining behavior is letting the user preview the destination of the back gesture before committing to it — meaning back destinations must be visually representable mid-gesture.
claims.quote: Android 13 (API level 33) introduces a predictive back gesture for Android devices such as phones, large screens, and foldables. The predictive back gesture is part of a multiyear release. When fully implemented, this feature lets users preview the destination or other result of a back gesture before they fully complete it, allowing them to decide whether to continue or stay in the current view.

claims.claim: Android's predictive back is defined as a preview-then-commit interaction: the back swipe reveals the destination before completion, letting the user abort mid-gesture — meaning the designer must design a partially-visible intermediate state, not just a discrete back transition.
claims.quote: Predictive back is the result of a gesture navigation operation in which a user has swiped back to preview their destination of the back gesture before fully completing it. This lets the user decide whether to continue—in other words, to "commit" to the back gesture—or stay in the current view.

claims.claim: Google instructs designers not to place touch targets or drag targets under the system gesture insets, which is the primary-source rule governing conflicts between author-built horizontal swipe affordances (carousels, swipe-to-delete) and the Android back gesture.
claims.quote: To help your users, predictive back navigation respects gesture insets defined in edge-to-edge features. Avoid adding touch gestures or drag targets under these gesture areas.

claims.claim: Predictive back is coupled to edge-to-edge: the guidance lists edge-to-edge support as a prerequisite, and predictive back's behavior is defined in terms of the gesture insets that edge-to-edge exposes.
claims.quote: Ensure your app has edge-to-edge support

claims.claim: Android specifies exact numeric motion values for the full-screen predictive-back transition: the exiting screen scales 100%→90%, the entering screen scales 110%→100%, and a fade-through crossover occurs at a 35% gesture-progress threshold where neither screen is visible.
claims.quote: For full screen surface transitions, there is a fade through progress threshold set at 35%. The progress threshold represents the progress value at which the exiting screen fully fades out and the entering screen starts to fade in. At the 35% mark, neither screen is showing.

claims.claim: Predictive back shared-element motion has a formulaic spacing spec — horizontal shift of ((screen width / 20) - 8) dp preserving an 8 dp screen-edge margin, minimum window scale 90%, and scale-down capped at 50% if the surface shifts off screen.
claims.quote: X shift: ((screen width / 20) - 8) dp — Maximum shift, leaves 8dp margin

claims.claim: Apple's HIG root page describes Liquid Glass in its own hero-card alt text as a transparent material applied to standard controls (toggles, sliders, buttons) that casts shadows on the background, lets underlying colored elements show through, and produces a "lensing" effect — i.e. Liquid Glass is a control-surface material, not a background wallpaper treatment.
claims.quote: An illustration of several Liquid Glass components such as toggles, sliders, and buttons, atop a neutral background. The transparent components cast shadows on the background and allow their colored elements, like a blue slider track and a green toggle backing, to show through, highlighting the Liquid Glass material's lensing effect.

claims.claim: Apple frames Liquid Glass as a layer that sits over background content and refracts/bends what is behind it, establishing depth by layering rather than by opacity — stated in the alt text of the Materials foundation thumbnail on the HIG root.
claims.quote: A sketch of a capsule shape overlapping a square. A subtle bend in the edges of the square that are beneath the capsule suggests the layering of the Liquid Glass material over background content.

claims.claim: Materials is a first-class HIG "foundation" for designers, ranked on the root page alongside Accessibility, App icons, Color, Layout, and Typography, and Apple defines a material as a visual effect creating depth, layering, and hierarchy between foreground and background elements.
claims.quote: A material is a visual effect that creates a sense of depth, layering, and hierarchy between foreground and background elements.

claims.claim: Google states Material 3 Expressive's research basis as 46 separate research studies with more than 18,000 participants worldwide, using eye tracking, surveys/focus groups, sentiment experiments, and usability testing.
claims.quote: Through 46 separate research studies with hundreds of designs, and more than 18,000 participants from around the world, we've fine tuned a system that's both beautiful and highly usable.

claims.claim: Google claims a measurable usability gain from Expressive styling: participants located key UI elements up to four times faster in M3 Expressive designs than in the non-expressive baseline.
claims.quote: Participants were able to spot key UI elements up to four times faster in the M3 Expressive designs

claims.claim: Google claims Expressive treatment erases an age-related speed gap: older users spotted key interactive elements as fast as younger users, tested across 10 apps.
claims.quote: Expressive design enabled older users to spot key interactive elements on the screen just as fast as younger users across 10 apps tested.

claims.claim: Preference for expressive designs was net-positive across all age groups and peaked at up to 87% among 18-to-24-year-olds — i.e. Google positions Expressive as demographically skewed, not universally preferred equally.
claims.quote: up to 87% — among 18-to-24-year-olds

claims.claim: Google explicitly constrains Expressive: visual flourish must not override clarity or core functionality, and removing established UI patterns (e.g. unlabeled icons, unstructured layouts) measurably decreased usability despite higher visual appeal.
claims.quote: Don't compromise your product's core functionality for visual flourishes. No amount of emotion can compensate for a lack of clarity.

claims.claim: Apple requires that a shortcut gesture (such as swipe-from-edge to go back) supplement rather than replace a tappable control: an app with a view hierarchy must still provide a Back button in the top toolbar, with the swipe offered only as an accelerator. This makes the iOS interactive pop gesture an addition to, never a substitute for, visible back navigation.
claims.quote: Use shortcut gestures to supplement standard gestures, not replace them. While you may supply a custom gesture to quickly access parts of your app, people also need simple, familiar ways to navigate and perform actions, even if it means an extra tap or two. For example, in an app that supports navigation through a hierarchy of views, people expect to find a Back button in a top toolbar that lets them return to the previous view with a single tap. To help accelerate this action, many apps also offer a shortcut gesture — such as swiping from the side of a window or touchscreen — while continuing to provide the Back button.

claims.claim: Apple instructs designers not to define custom gestures that conflict with system-UI access gestures, and permits deferring a system gesture only in narrow cases (games or immersive experiences) — not in ordinary app UI. This is the primary-source rule governing author-built horizontal swipe affordances that collide with system edge gestures.
claims.quote: Avoid conflicting with gestures that access system UI. Several platforms offer gestures for accessing system behaviors, like edge swiping in watchOS or rolling your hand over to access system overlays in visionOS. It’s important to avoid defining custom gestures that might conflict with these interactions, as people expect these controls to work consistently. In specific circumstances within games or immersive experiences, developers can work around this area by deferring the system gesture.

claims.claim: Apple sets four mandatory properties for any custom gesture, including that it must never be the only way to perform an important action — so a swipe-only affordance (e.g. swipe-to-delete with no alternative) violates HIG unless a non-gesture path exists.
claims.quote: Add custom gestures only when necessary. Custom gestures work best when you design them for specialized tasks that people perform frequently and that aren’t covered by existing gestures, like in a game or drawing app. If you decide to implement a custom gesture, make sure it’s: Discoverable Straightforward to perform Distinct from other gestures Not the only way to perform an important action in your app or game

claims.claim: Apple defines swipe as a standard gesture supported on all six platforms whose canonical meanings are revealing actions/controls, dismissing views, and scrolling — establishing swipe-to-reveal-actions (swipe-to-delete) and swipe-to-dismiss-sheet as system-sanctioned conventions rather than app inventions, and forbidding redefinition of swipe for app-unique actions.
claims.quote: Avoid using a familiar gesture like tap or swipe to perform an action that’s unique to your app; similarly, avoid creating a unique gesture to perform a standard action like activating a button or scrolling a long view.

claims.claim: On iOS and iPadOS, Apple reserves specific multi-finger gestures that designers must not reassign: three-finger swipe = undo/redo, three-finger pinch = copy/paste, four-finger swipe (iPadOS only) = switch apps, shake = undo/redo.
claims.quote: In addition to the [standard gestures] supported in all platforms, iOS and iPadOS support a few other gestures that people expect. Gesture Common action Three-finger swipe Initiate undo (left swipe); initiate redo (right swipe). Three-finger pinch Copy selected text (pinch in); paste copied text (pinch out). Four-finger swipe (iPadOS only) Switch between apps. Shake Initiate undo; initiate redo.

claims.claim: In iOS, Apple's tab bar is a floating bottom element rendered on the Liquid Glass material, not an opaque bar pinned to the screen edge — the material is explicitly specified to let underlying content show through.
claims.quote: A tab bar floats above content at the bottom of the screen. Its items rest on a [Liquid Glass] background that allows content beneath to peek through.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits using tab bars for actions: tab bars are for navigation between top-level app sections only, and controls acting on the current view belong in a toolbar instead.
claims.quote: Use a tab bar to support navigation, not to provide actions. A tab bar lets people navigate among different sections of an app, like the Alarm, Stopwatch, and Timer tabs in the Clock app. If you need to provide controls that act on elements in the current view, use a [toolbar] instead.

claims.claim: Apple requires the tab bar to stay visible during in-app navigation (modals being the sole exception), and forbids disabling or hiding individual tab buttons even when their content is empty.
claims.quote: Make sure the tab bar is visible when people navigate to different sections of your app. If you hide the tab bar, people can forget which area of the app they're in. The exception is when a modal view covers the tab bar, because a modal is temporary and self-contained. […] Don't disable or hide tab bar buttons, even when their content is unavailable. Having tab bar buttons available in some cases but not others makes your app's interface appear unstable and unpredictable. If a section is empty, explain why its content is unavailable.

claims.claim: iOS and iPadOS place the tab bar in structurally different locations — bottom of screen on iOS versus near the top on iPadOS, where it can optionally convert to a sidebar — so a single tab-bar layout cannot serve both idioms unchanged. Apple caps customizable tab sets at five or fewer for continuity across size classes.
claims.quote: The system displays a tab bar near the top of the screen. You can choose to have the tab bar appear as a fixed element, or with a button that converts it to a sidebar. […] If you let people select their own tabs, aim for a default list of five or fewer to preserve continuity between compact and regular view sizes.

claims.claim: Apple gives no fixed maximum tab count for iOS/iPadOS but instructs designers to avoid overflow, because exceeding the horizontal space converts the trailing tab into a 'More' tab that hides content; iOS also defines a dedicated trailing search tab and a scroll-triggered minimized tab bar state for attached accessories.
claims.quote: Avoid overflow tabs. […] If horizontal space limits the number of visible tabs, the trailing tab becomes a More tab in iOS and iPadOS, revealing the remaining items in a separate list. The More tab makes it harder for people to reach and notice content on tabs that are hidden, so limit scenarios in your app where this can happen. […] A tab bar can include a dedicated search tab at the trailing end.

claims.claim: Apple defines exactly two system detents for iOS/iPadOS sheets — large (full expanded height) and medium (about half of full height) — and the expansion behavior is asymmetric: large is always supported by default, adding medium yields a two-rest-height sheet, and specifying medium alone blocks the sheet from ever reaching full height. Custom detent values are also permitted.
claims.quote: The system defines two detents: large is the height of a fully expanded sheet and medium is about half of the fully expanded height. Sheets can have one or more custom detent values. [...] Sheets automatically support the large detent. Adding the medium detent allows the sheet to rest at both heights, whereas specifying only medium prevents the sheet from expanding to full height.

claims.claim: Apple specifies vertical swipe as the user-expected dismissal gesture for iOS/iPadOS sheets — not a dismiss button — and mandates an action sheet confirmation when the swipe begins with unsaved changes present. This establishes the vertical axis as system-claimed inside sheets, constraining author-built vertical drag affordances there.
claims.quote: Support swiping to dismiss a sheet. People expect to swipe vertically to dismiss a sheet instead of tapping a dismiss button. If people have unsaved changes in the sheet when they begin swiping to dismiss it, use an action sheet to let them confirm their action.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits stacked/nested sheets from the main interface: only one sheet may be displayed at a time, and a sheet that triggers another sheet must be closed before the new one appears (it may be redisplayed after the second is dismissed). Stated rationale is that returning from a sheet to another sheet destroys the user's sense of location.
claims.quote: Display only one sheet at a time from the main interface. When people close a sheet, they expect to return to the parent view or window. If closing a sheet takes people back to another sheet, they can lose track of where they are in your app. If something people do within a sheet results in another sheet appearing, close the first sheet before displaying the new one.

claims.claim: As of the March 24, 2026 revision, Apple prescribes concrete button placement law for iOS/iPadOS sheets: Cancel on the leading edge of the top toolbar, Done on the trailing edge; in multi-step flows Back replaces Cancel on subsequent steps and Done stays inactive until the final step; and Cancel, Done, and Back must never be shown together.
claims.quote: In iOS and iPadOS, for sheets with a single view, the Cancel button belongs on the leading edge of the top toolbar. When present, the Done button belongs on the trailing edge. [...] On subsequent steps, the Back button replaces the Cancel button to let people navigate back. On the final confirmation step, the Done button becomes active [...] Avoid showing all three buttons — Cancel, Done, and Back — together.

claims.claim: Sheet modality is not uniform across Apple platforms — macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS sheets are always modal, while only iOS and iPadOS permit a nonmodal sheet that affects the parent view without being dismissed — and iPadOS specifically should use the page or form sheet presentation styles, which center content over a dimmed background at a default size rather than emerging edge-to-edge from the bottom.
claims.quote: In macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS, a sheet is always modal. [...] In iOS and iPadOS, a sheet can be either modal or nonmodal. [...] Prefer using the page or form sheet presentation styles in an iPadOS app. Each style uses a default size for the sheet, centering its content on top of a dimmed background view and providing a consistent experience.

claims.claim: For apps targeting Android 16 (API 36), edge-to-edge is fully mandatory: the Android 15 opt-out attribute R.attr#windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement is deprecated and disabled on Android 16 devices, so a designer cannot assume opaque system bars will reserve space — every layout must be designed to draw beneath the status and navigation bars and handle window insets.
claims.quote: For apps targeting Android 16 (API level 36), `R.attr#windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement` is deprecated and disabled, and your app can't opt-out of going edge-to-edge.

claims.claim: The edge-to-edge opt-out is version-conditional, not app-conditional: an app targeting API 36 still honors windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement when it runs on an Android 15 device, so the same build can render with and without system-bar insets depending on the OS it lands on.
claims.quote: If your app targets Android 16 (API level 36) and is running on an Android 15 device, `R.attr#windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement` continues to work.

claims.claim: Predictive back system animations (back-to-home, cross-task, cross-activity) are on by default for apps targeting Android 16, and the legacy back path is dead — onBackPressed is not called and KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK is not dispatched — meaning Android's system back gesture now owns a previewing animation that any author-built horizontal swipe affordance must not fight.
claims.quote: For apps targeting Android 16 (API level 36) or higher and running on an Android 16 or higher device, the predictive back system animations (back-to-home, cross-task, and cross-activity) are enabled by default. Additionally, `onBackPressed` is not called and [`KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK`](/reference/android/view/KeyEvent#KEYCODE_BACK) is not dispatched anymore.

claims.claim: Predictive back retains a temporary escape hatch that edge-to-edge does not: apps can set android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="false" on the <application> or <activity> tag to opt out while migrating.
claims.quote: or temporarily opt out by setting the [`android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback`](/guide/topics/manifest/activity-element#enableOnBackInvokedCallback) attribute to `false` in the `<application>` or `<activity>` tag of your app's `AndroidManifest.xml` file.

claims.claim: On displays with smallest width >= 600dp, Android 16 ignores screenOrientation, resizableActivity, minAspectRatio and maxAspectRatio — apps fill the whole display window with no pillarboxing — so a designer can no longer lock a phone-shaped portrait layout on tablets and foldables; the per-activity/application PROPERTY_COMPAT_ALLOW_RESTRICTED_RESIZABILITY opt-out stops working at API level 37.
claims.quote: For apps targeting Android 16 (API level 36), orientation, resizability, and aspect ratio restrictions no longer apply on displays with smallest width >= 600dp. Apps fill the entire display window, regardless of aspect ratio or a user's preferred orientation, and pillarboxing isn't used.

claims.claim: Material 3 makes the navigation rail vs. navigation bar choice a function of Android window size class, not designer preference: compact windows (under 600dp) must use a navigation bar, medium (600–839dp) and larger use a rail, and the two must never coexist.
claims.quote: Never use the navigation rail and navigation bar simultaneously. Only use navigation rails for medium window size classes and larger. … Compact: Don’t use a standard navigation rail for compact layouts due to space constraints. Use a navigation bar instead. … [medium =] Window widths from 600dp to 839dp, such as a tablet or foldable in portrait orientation.

claims.claim: The collapsed navigation rail is specified to contain 3–7 navigation items, run along the leading edge, and must not be hidden; above five destinations M3 directs designers to a modal expanded rail.
claims.quote: The collapsed nav rail runs along the leading edge of the window, and should contain 3–7 navigation items. It should not be hidden. … If there are more than five destinations, consider using a modal expanded nav rail instead.

claims.claim: Android predictive back applies to the navigation rail only in its modal expanded configuration — the collapsed rail and the standard (non-modal) expanded rail are not dismissed by the back gesture.
claims.quote: On Android, a gesture called predictive back allows people to swipe left or right on the screen to go back or dismiss modal components. … Predictive back only applies to the modal expanded navigation rail.

claims.claim: In the Material 3 Expressive update the navigation drawer is superseded by the expanded navigation rail as the recommended large-window navigation component.
claims.quote: Navigation drawers let people switch between UI views on larger devices. In the expressive update, use an expanded navigation rail.

claims.claim: The rail's placement is a hard constraint, not a layout option: it must be vertical, on the leading edge (left in LTR, right in RTL), outside any panes, and Material explicitly forbids using it horizontally.
claims.quote: The navigation rail should be placed on the leading edge of the window. This is the left side for left-to-right languages, and the right side for right-to-left languages. … Don’t use the navigation rail horizontally. claims.quote: For tab bars with an attached accessory, like the MiniPlayer in Music, you can choose to minimize the tab bar and move the accessory inline with it when a person scrolls down. A person can exit the minimized state by tapping a tab or scrolling to the top of the view.

claims.claim: Apple places the tab bar at a DIFFERENT screen edge per platform: bottom on iOS, but near the top on iPadOS, where it can optionally convert to a sidebar via a button. Apple further caps a customizable default tab list at five or fewer. This is a hard divergence from Android, where the navigation bar is always bottom-anchored and the large-screen equivalent is a navigation rail.
claims.quote: The system displays a tab bar near the top of the screen. You can choose to have the tab bar appear as a fixed element, or with a button that converts it to a sidebar. ... If you let people select their own tabs, aim for a default list of five or fewer to preserve continuity between compact and regular view sizes.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits using the tab bar for actions — it is strictly for top-level navigation, and controls that act on the current view belong in a toolbar instead. Apple also prohibits hiding the tab bar during navigation (only a covering modal may obscure it) and prohibits disabling or hiding individual tab buttons when their content is empty.
claims.quote: Use a tab bar to support navigation, not to provide actions. ... If you need to provide controls that act on elements in the current view, use a toolbar instead. ... Don't disable or hide tab bar buttons, even when their content is unavailable. Having tab bar buttons available in some cases but not others makes your app's interface appear unstable and unpredictable.

claims.claim: Apple does not state a fixed maximum tab count for iOS; instead, overflow is handled automatically — when horizontal space runs out, the trailing tab becomes a 'More' tab in iOS and iPadOS, and Apple explicitly directs designers to avoid triggering this. Apple additionally warns against tab label colors that lack contrast against content-layer backgrounds, recommending a monochromatic tab bar over colorful content (a Liquid Glass legibility constraint).
claims.quote: Avoid overflow tabs. Depending on device size and orientation, the number of visible tabs can be smaller than the total number of tabs. If horizontal space limits the number of visible tabs, the trailing tab becomes a More tab in iOS and iPadOS, revealing the remaining items in a separate list. ... If your app already has bright, colorful content in the content layer, prefer a monochromatic appearance for tab bars, or choose an accent color with sufficient visual differentiation.

When a nonmodal sheet is onscreen, people use its functionality to affect the parent view without dismissing the sheet.

For example, in an app that supports navigation through a hierarchy of views, people expect to find a Back button in a top toolbar that lets them return to the previous view with a single tap. It's important to avoid defining custom gestures that might conflict with these interactions, as people expect these controls to work consistently. In specific circumstances within games or immersive experiences, developers can work around this area by deferring the system gesture.

For example, people expect tap to activate or select an object. Avoid using a familiar gesture like tap or swipe to perform an action that's unique to your app; similarly, avoid creating a unique gesture to perform a standard action like activating a button or scrolling a long view.

claims.claim: Apple's HIG Accessibility page specifies iOS/iPadOS control sizing as a DEFAULT of 44x44 pt and a MINIMUM of 28x28 pt — meaning the widely repeated "Apple requires 44pt minimum touch targets" is a restatement of Apple's *default*, not its stated floor. (watchOS is also 44x44 default / 28x28 min; macOS 28x28 default / 20x20 min; tvOS 66x66 / 56x56; visionOS 60x60 / 28x28.)
claims.quote: Offer sufficiently sized controls. Controls that are too small are hard for many people to interact with and select. Strive to meet the recommended minimum control size for each platform to ensure controls and menus are comfortable for all when tapping and clicking. [Table] Platform | Default control size | Minimum control size — iOS, iPadOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt — macOS | 28x28 pt | 20x20 pt — tvOS | 66x66 pt | 56x56 pt — visionOS | 60x60 pt | 28x28 pt — watchOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt

claims.claim: Apple specifies a body/default type size of 17 pt for iOS and iPadOS with an absolute minimum of 11 pt, and gives per-platform defaults/minimums (macOS 13/10, tvOS 29/23, visionOS 17/12, watchOS 16/12). This is the primary-source figure for iOS default body text size.
claims.quote: Use recommended defaults for custom type sizes. Each platform has different default and minimum sizes for system-defined type styles to promote readability. If you're using custom type styles, follow the recommended defaults. [Table] Platform | Default size | Minimum size — iOS, iPadOS | 17 pt | 11 pt — macOS | 13 pt | 10 pt — tvOS | 29 pt | 23 pt — visionOS | 17 pt | 12 pt — watchOS | 16 pt | 12 pt

claims.claim: Apple gives a concrete spacing baseline for interactive elements: approximately 12 points of padding around bezeled elements and approximately 24 points around non-bezeled elements, and states spacing matters as much as target size.
claims.quote: Consider spacing between controls as important as size. Include enough padding between elements to reduce the chance that someone taps the wrong control. In general, it works well to add about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel. For elements without a bezel, about 24 points of padding works well around the element's visible edges.

claims.claim: Apple adopts WCAG Level AA contrast values as its guidance: 4.5:1 minimum for text up to 17 pt (all weights), and 3:1 for text at 18 pt or for bold text at any size — and requires a higher-contrast scheme when the system Increase Contrast setting is on if defaults don't meet this.
claims.quote: Two popular standards of measure for color contrast are the [WCAG] and the Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA). ... uses the following values from WCAG Level AA as guidance in determining whether your app's colors have an acceptable contrast. [Table] Text size | Text weight | Minimum contrast ratio — Up to 17 pts | All | 4.5:1 — 18 pts | All | 3:1 — All | Bold | 3:1. If your app doesn't provide this minimum contrast by default, ensure it at least provides a higher contrast color scheme when the system setting Increase Contrast is turned on.

claims.claim: Apple sets a quantified text-scaling target: interfaces should let people enlarge text by at least 200 percent (140 percent on watchOS), achievable via Dynamic Type or custom UI — a hard constraint on layout decisions a designer must accommodate.
claims.quote: Support larger text sizes. Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type.

claims.claim: Edge-to-edge layout is stated as a first-class requirement for gesture-navigation compatibility, tying Android's gesture system directly to the safe-area/inset design problem; exclusion regions are meanwhile to be used only when genuinely necessary.
claims.quote: Extend app content from edge to edge. ... Games must make sure to only exclude these areas when necessary, such as during gameplay.

claims.quote: Predictive back is the result of a gesture navigation operation in which a user has swiped back to preview their destination of the back gesture before fully completing it. This lets the user decide whether to continue—in other words, to 'commit' to the back gesture—or stay in the current view.

claims.claim: Google explicitly forbids placing author-built touch gestures or drag targets inside the system gesture inset areas, which is the primary rule governing conflicts between the Android back-swipe and horizontal swipe affordances such as carousels or swipe-to-delete.
claims.quote: To help your users, predictive back navigation respects gesture insets defined in edge-to-edge features. Avoid adding touch gestures or drag targets under these gesture areas.

claims.claim: Even where a back preview lets the user directly manipulate a detached surface, Android forbids designing that surface so it reads as a swipe-to-dismiss of an item — back must not be visually conflated with item dismissal.
claims.quote: However, the design shouldn't visually suggest to the user that completing a back gesture dismisses an item in the direction of the back gesture.

claims.claim: Android specifies exact numeric motion values for a full-screen predictive-back preview: the exiting surface scales 100%→90%, the entering surface 110%→100%, with a fade-through crossover at 35% gesture progress where neither screen is visible, using interpolator parameters (.1, .1, 0, 1) to match SystemUI.
claims.quote: For full screen surface transitions, there is a fade through progress threshold set at 35%. The progress threshold represents the progress value at which the exiting screen fully fades out and the entering screen starts to fade in. At the 35% mark, neither screen is showing.

claims.claim: Shared-element predictive-back shifts are computed from screen dimensions with a fixed 8 dp edge margin — x-shift = ((screen width / 20) - 8) dp, e.g. 56 dp on a 1280-wide screen — and the surface scales to no less than 90% of window size.
claims.quote: If the screen width is 1280, making the x-shift 56 dp. The formula for that is: ((1280/20)-8) = 56 dp x-shift

claims.claim: Android's design guidance defines edge-to-edge as drawing app UI underneath the system bars, and prescribes a split rule: backgrounds and divider lines extend fully to the screen edges while text and buttons are inset away from system UI and hardware elements.
claims.quote: An edge-to-edge app takes advantage of the entire screen by drawing UI under the system bars. ... In general, backgrounds and divider lines should also draw edge-to-edge while content like text and buttons should be inset to avoid the system UI and hardware elements.

claims.claim: Android specifies three distinct inset types a designer must reason about separately — system bar insets (tappable, must not be visually obscured), system gesture insets (OS gesture-navigation areas that take priority over the app), and display cutout insets (camera cutout and similar intrusions into the display surface).
claims.quote: System bar insets apply to UI that is both tappable and shouldn't be visually obscured by the system bars. ... System gesture insets apply to gesture-navigational areas used by the OS that take priority over your app. ... Display cutout insets apply to device areas that extend into the display surface, such as the camera cutout.

claims.claim: Android explicitly prohibits placing tap gestures or drag targets under system insets because they conflict with edge-to-edge layout and gesture navigation — the direct platform statement on the gesture-conflict problem for author-built swipe affordances.
claims.quote: Avoid adding tap gestures or drag targets under system insets; these conflict with edge-to-edge and gesture navigation.

claims.claim: Status bar treatment under edge-to-edge is conditional on navigation mode and app-bar behavior: status bars must be translucent when content scrolls beneath them (via Material 3 TopAppBar protection or a matching gradient), a scrim is added for three-button navigation when the bottom app bar animates away, and gesture navigation must be left transparent with no additional scrim.
claims.quote: Status bars should be translucent when the UI scrolls underneath, so that the status bar icons don't look cluttered. ... Add system bar scrim for three-button navigation when the bottom app bar animates away. ... Keep gesture navigation transparent and don't add an additional scrim.

claims.claim: For display cutouts, Android directs designers to inset critical UI using display cutout insets and never place critical UI at the very screen edge, while solid app bar backgrounds and horizontal carousels should deliberately draw into the cutout region.
claims.quote: Inset critical UI using display cutout insets. ... Place critical UI at the very edge of the screen. [Don't] ... Ensure horizontal carousels draw into the display cutout.

claims.claim: The default drawing behavior changed by API level: on Android 14 (API 34) and lower the app UI does not draw underneath system bars and display cutouts by default, while on Android 15 (API 35)+ targeting SDK 35 it does.
